claim: Persistent firing in lateral entorhinal cortex layer III (LEC III) supports temporal associative learning.
source: Whether and how persistent firing in lateral entorhinal cortex layer III (LEC III) supports temporal associative learning is still unknown.
evidence: The manuscript states this is unknown, indicating it is a research question rather than a supported claim at the outset.

claim: Persistent firing ability from neurons from behaviorally naive aged rats was lower compared to neurons from young rats.
source: Persistent firing ability from neurons from behaviorally naive aged rats was lower compared to neurons from young rats.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in Figure 1 and Tables 1-2.

claim: Neurons from learning impaired aged animals exhibited reduced persistent firing capacity.
source: Neurons from learning impaired aged animals also exhibited reduced persistent firing capacity, which may contribute to aging-related learning impairments.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2 and associated tables.

claim: Reduced persistent firing capacity may contribute to aging-related learning impairments.
source: Neurons from learning impaired aged animals also exhibited reduced persistent firing capacity, which may contribute to aging-related learning impairments.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the correlation between reduced persistent firing and learning impairments.

claim: Successful acquisition of the trace eyeblink task increased persistent firing ability in both young and aged rats.
source: Successful acquisition of the trace eyeblink task, however, increased persistent firing ability in both young and aged rats.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing conditioned vs. pseudoconditioned and unimpaired vs. impaired groups.

claim: Changes in persistent firing ability are due to changes to the afterdepolarization.
source: These changes in persistent firing ability are due to changes to the afterdepolarization, which may in turn be modulated by the postburst afterhyperpolarization.
evidence: This is supported by experimental measurements of ADP and correlations with persistent firing properties.

claim: The afterdepolarization may be modulated by the postburst afterhyperpolarization.
source: These changes in persistent firing ability are due to changes to the afterdepolarization, which may in turn be modulated by the postburst afterhyperpolarization.
evidence: This is speculative based on observed correlations between AHP and ADP.

claim: Successful learning increases persistent firing ability.
source: Together, these data indicate that successful learning increases persistent firing ability and decreases in persistent firing ability contribute to learning impairments in aging.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing learning groups.

claim: Decreases in persistent firing ability contribute to learning impairments in aging.
source: Together, these data indicate that successful learning increases persistent firing ability and decreases in persistent firing ability contribute to learning impairments in aging.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between persistent firing deficits and learning impairments in aged animals.

claim: Persistent firing is the ability of a neuron to continuously fire action potentials even after the termination of a triggering stimulus.
source: Persistent firing is the ability of a neuron to continuously fire action potentials even after the termination of a triggering stimulus.
evidence: This is a definition based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Temporal associative learning and other working memory-dependent tasks are thought to rely on persistent firing because this mechanism may serve to bridge the temporal gap between task-relevant stimulus presentation and the execution of a learned response.
source: Temporal associative learning and other working memory-dependent tasks are thought to rely on persistent firing because this mechanism may serve to bridge the temporal gap between task-relevant stimulus presentation and the execution of a learned response (Zylberberg and Strowbridge, 2017; Tsao et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Evidence that persistent firing may support temporal associative learning comes from an in vivo study of prefrontal neurons, which showed elevated activity during the delay period of a working memory task.
source: Evidence that persistent firing may support temporal associative learning comes from an in vivo study of prefrontal neurons, which showed elevated activity during the delay period of a working memory task (Fuster, 1972).
evidence: This is supported by citation to Fuster, 1972.

claim: The lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) has been shown to be important for temporal associative learning.
source: One region that has been shown to be important for temporal associative learning is the lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) (Morrissey et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Persistent firing in the LEC is dependent upon cholinergic activation.
source: In vitro, persistent firing in the LEC is dependent upon cholinergic activation (Tahvildari et al., 2007; Tahvildari et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous in vitro studies.

claim: Application of a cholinergic antagonist into the entorhinal cortex impairs the acquisition of temporal associative learning tasks such as trace fear and trace eyeblink conditioning.
source: Application of a cholinergic antagonist into the entorhinal cortex impairs the acquisition of temporal associative learning tasks such as trace fear and trace eyeblink conditioning (Esclassan et al., 2009; Tanninen et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Within the LEC, layers III and V pyramidal neurons have been shown to be capable of persistent firing.
source: Within the LEC, layers III and V pyramidal neurons have been shown to be capable of persistent firing (Tahvildari et al., 2007; Tahvildari et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Layer III pyramidal neurons integrate and provide object information directly to the CA1 region of the hippocampus, forming the temporoammonic pathway.
source: Notably, layer III pyramidal neurons integrate and provide object information directly to the CA1 region of the hippocampus, forming the temporoammonic pathway (van Groen et al., 2003; Hargreaves et al., 2005; Deshmukh and Knierim, 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous anatomical and functional studies.

claim: Persistent firing by layer III LEC pyramidal neurons is a prime candidate to support temporal associative learning.
source: Thus, persistent firing by layer III LEC pyramidal neurons is a prime candidate to support temporal associative learning.
evidence: This is an inference based on the anatomical connectivity and functional properties described.

claim: The LEC is highly susceptible to aging-related changes.
source: Along with its role in hippocampus-dependent learning, the LEC is also highly susceptible to aging-related changes.
evidence: This is supported by subsequent citations about tau pathology and structural changes.

claim: The LEC is the initial site of Alzheimer's-related tau pathology in cortical regions.
source: The LEC is the initial site of Alzheimer's-related tau pathology in cortical regions (Moryś et al., 1994; Gómez-Isla et al., 1996; Stranahan and Mattson, 2010; Khan et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous pathological studies.

claim: Changes to LEC structure and activity in normal aging is associated with learning and other cognitive impairments.
source: Several studies have also determined that changes to LEC structure and activity in normal aging is associated with learning and other cognitive impairments (Rodrigue and Raz, 2004; Yassa et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: LEC hypoactivity has been shown to be associated with impairments in pattern separation in aging humans.
source: For example, LEC hypoactivity has been shown to be associated with impairments in pattern separation in aging humans (Reagh et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a previous study.

claim: There may be alterations to persistent firing ability in LEC III that may contribute to the aging-related learning impairments.
source: As a result of its susceptibility to aging, there may be alterations to persistent firing ability in LEC III that may contribute to the aging-related learning impairments we and others have observed (Thompson et al., 1996; Knuttinen et al., 2001; Tombaugh et al., 2005; Disterhoft and Oh, 2006; Galvez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a hypothesis supported by citations to previous observations of aging-related learning impairments.

claim: Neurons from AN animals had a lower probability of persistent firing compared to neurons from YN rats when injected with a 100 pA and a 150 pA stimulus.
source: Neurons from AN animals had a lower probability of persistent firing compared to neurons from YN rats, which were able to fire close to 100%, when injected with a 100 pA and a 150 pA stimulus (Figure 1B; Table 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B and Table 1.

claim: When persistent firing was evoked in neurons from YN and AN rats with a 2 s long train of 2 ms, 2 nA current pulses at 20 Hz, neurons from AN rats had a lower probability of firing compared to neurons from YN rats.
source: When persistent firing was evoked in neurons from YN and AN rats with this protocol, neurons from AN rats again had a lower probability of firing compared to neurons from YN rats, which were able to fire at nearly 100% (Figure 1D; Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D and Table 2.

claim: Persistent firing was able to be evoked in neurons from YN and AN rats using a 250 ms long current injection with the membrane potentials held at 2 mV and 5 mV more hyperpolarized than spontaneous firing threshold.
source: Persistent firing was able to be evoked in neurons from YN and AN rats using a 250 ms long current injection with the membrane potentials held at 2 mV and 5 mV more hyperpolarized than spontaneous firing threshold.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and 1H.

claim: With the membrane potential at 2 mV more hyperpolarized, the firing probability of neurons from YN animals was 100%, although it was again lower in neurons from AN.
source: With the membrane potential at 2 mV more hyperpolarized, the firing probability of neurons from YN animals was 100%, although it was again lower in neurons from AN (Figure 1F; Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F and Table 2.

claim: When the neuronal membrane potential was held at 5 mV below spontaneous firing threshold, the probability of firing was lower for neurons in both groups overall, and there was no statistical difference in probability between the young and aged groups.
source: When the neuronal membrane potential was held at 5 mV below spontaneous firing threshold, the probability of firing was lower for neurons in both groups overall, and there was no statistical difference in probability between the young and aged groups (Figure 1H; Table 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1H and Table 2.

claim: Neurons from behaviorally naive aged animals overall have a lower probability of persistent firing compared to neurons from young animals.
source: Together, these data indicate that neurons from behaviorally naive aged animals overall have a lower probability of persistent firing compared to neurons from young animals, which were nearly always able to fire persistently.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion supported by the experimental data in Figure 1 and Tables 1-2.

claim: The decreased probability of firing from aged animals may contribute to the aging-related learning impairments in trace eyeblink conditioning.
source: The decreased probability of firing from aged animals may contribute to the aging-related learning impairments in trace eyeblink conditioning that we have previously observed (Thompson et al., 1996; Knuttinen et al., 2001; Disterhoft and Oh, 2006; Galvez et al., 2011).
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between persistent firing deficits and previously observed learning impairments.

claim: The aged rats were separated into aged impaired (AI) or aged unimpaired (AU) groups based upon whether they achieved a 60% conditioned response (CR) learning criterion.
source: The aged rats were separated into aged impaired (AI) or aged unimpaired (AU) groups based upon whether they achieved a 60% conditioned response (CR) learning criterion.
evidence: This is a methodological statement describing the experimental design.

claim: YC and AU animals successfully acquire trace eyeblink conditioning.
source: Our learning curves show a steady increase across the training sessions in % CRs from the groups that were trained on the trace eyeblink conditioning paradigm and were able to acquire it (YC and AU)
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B and Table 3.

claim: YP and AI animals did not exhibit a discernable increase in % CR.
source: YP and AI animals did not exhibit a discernable increase in % CR.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: YC rats showed the fastest rate of increase in % CR, exhibiting more CRs within the first session than YP, AI, or even AU.
source: YC rats showed the fastest rate of increase in % CR, exhibiting more CRs within the first session than YP, AI, or even AU.
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B and Table 3.

claim: Although AU were slower than YC rats in learning trace eyeblink conditioning, they were indiscernible from YC in terms of % CR by the end of training.
source: Although AU were slower than YC rats in learning trace eyeblink conditioning, they were indiscernible from YC in terms of % CR by the end of training (Figure 2B; Table 3).
evidence: This is supported by behavioral data shown in Figure 2B and Table 3.

claim: Neurons from AU animals were able to reach the same ceiling effect that we observed in young animals when the neuronal membrane potential was held at 2 mV more hyperpolarized than spontaneous firing threshold.
source: Neurons from AU animals were also able to reach the same ceiling effect that we observed in young animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Table 4.

claim: Neurons from AI had a lower probability of firing compared to AU, YC, and YP when the membrane potential was held at 2 mV more hyperpolarized than spontaneous firing threshold.
source: Neurons from AI, however, had a lower probability of firing compared to AU, YC, and YP (Kruskal-Wallis, H = 15.27, p=0.0016) (Figure 2C; Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2C and Table 4.

claim: Successful acquisition of trace eyeblink conditioning significantly increased the probability of firing at 5 mV below spontaneous firing threshold from both young adult and aged animals.
source: Successful acquisition of trace eyeblink conditioning, however, significantly increased the probability of firing at this membrane potential from both young adult and aged animals (Kruskal-Wallis, H = 30.86, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Table 4.

claim: In YC, neurons reached 100% firing when the membrane potential was held at 5 mV below spontaneous firing threshold.
source: In YC, neurons reached 100% firing, while neurons from YP had a lower probability, firing at levels similar to those of behaviorally naïve young animals (Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Table 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and supplementary figures.

claim: AU did not achieve the same ceiling level of firing as YC but were statistically comparable to YC as well as to YP.
source: Although AU did not achieve the same ceiling level of firing as YC, they were statistically comparable to YC as well as to YP (Figure 2D; Table 4)
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Table 4.

claim: AU had increased firing ability relative to neurons from AI and AN animals.
source: and had increased firing ability relative to neurons from AI and AN animals (Figure 2D; Table 4; Figure 2—figure supplement 1; Table 5).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and supplementary figures.

claim: AI had the lowest probability of firing relative to the other groups.
source: AI had the lowest probability of firing relative to the other groups (Figure 2D; Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2D and Table 4.

claim: Neurons from YC are the most active and have the highest spike count per cell across time.
source: Neurons from YC are the most active and have the highest spike count per cell across time.
evidence: This is supported by the raster plot analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: Neurons from AI are the least active and have the lowest spike count per cell across time.
source: In contrast, neurons from AI are the least active and have the lowest spike count per cell across time (Figure 3).
evidence: This is supported by the raster plot analysis shown in Figure 3.

claim: AI was the only group that did not have a ceiling or near-ceiling firing probability when persistent firing was evoked using a 2 s long 20 Hz train of current pulses.
source: When we evoked persistent firing using this protocol, AI again was the only group that did not have a ceiling or near-ceiling firing probability (Kruskal-Wallis, H = 12.00, p=0.0074) (Figure 2E, Table 4).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2E and Table 4.

claim: The mean rate of persistent firing was significantly reduced in LEC III pyramidal neurons from AN animals compared to those from YN animals.
source: In behaviorally naive animals, the mean rate of persistent firing was significantly reduced in LEC III pyramidal neurons from AN animals compared to those from YN animals (Figure 4B; Table 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B and Table 7.

claim: Firing rate increased over time, with the firing rate from neurons from YN animals rising faster over time compared to neurons from AN animals.
source: Firing rate also increased over time (RM ANOVA, F2.244, 67.31 = 43.81, p<0.0001), with the firing rate from neurons from YN animals rising faster over time compared to neurons from AN animals (F1,30 = 5.687, p=0.0236).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neurons from YN animals reached a peak of 6.45 ± 0.63 spikes/sec at the 9–10 s bin.
source: Neurons from YN animals reached a peak of 6.45 ± 0.63 spikes/sec at the 9–10 s bin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Neurons from AN animals only reached a peak of 4.20 ± 0.67 spikes/sec at the 19–20 s bin.
source: Neurons from AN animals, however, only reached a peak of 4.20 ± 0.67 spikes/sec at the 19–20 s bin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A one phase exponential decay function fit to the rising phase of the firing rate (0–9 s) revealed a time constant of 2.66 s for neurons from YN animals, but a time constant of 4.72 s for neurons from AN animals.
source: A one phase exponential decay function (Y(t)=Ymax (1 - e-t/τ)) fit to the rising phase of the firing rate (0–9 s) averaged across all neurons revealed a time constant of 2.66 s for neurons from YN animals, but a time constant of 4.72 s for neurons from AN animals (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and curve fitting shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Learning changed the mean rate of persistent firing.
source: Learning also changed the mean rate of persistent firing (ANOVA, F3, 55 = 14.00, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: Neurons from YC had a faster rate of firing compared to YP, AU, and AI.
source: However, neurons from YC had a faster rate of firing compared to YP, AU, and AI (Figure 4D; Table 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Table 9.

claim: The persistent firing rate of neurons from AU animals was not statistically different from neurons of AI animals.
source: In fact, the persistent firing rate of neurons from AU animals was not statistically different from neurons of AI animals, although they did fire faster than neurons from AN animals (Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Table 8).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures and tables.

claim: There was a significant positive correlation between behavior and persistent firing rate amongst the aged group (AU, AI) that was not present amongst the YC group.
source: Despite the slower firing rate from the aged group of animals, there was a significant positive correlation between behavior and persistent firing rate amongst the aged group (AU, AI) that was not present amongst the YC group (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Neurons from YC animals reached a peak of 10.92 ± 0.74 spikes/sec at the 5–6 s bin.
source: Neurons from YC animals reached a peak of 10.92 ± 0.74 spikes/sec at the 5–6 s bin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Neurons from YP animals were only able to reach a peak firing rate of 7.76 ± 0.73 spikes/sec at the 8–9 s bin.
source: Neurons from YP animals were only able to reach a peak firing rate of 7.76 ± 0.73 spikes/sec at the 8–9 s bin, however, indicating that learning caused persistent firing rate to increase faster (Table 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D and Table 9.

claim: Learning caused persistent firing rate to increase faster.
source: Neurons from YP animals were only able to reach a peak firing rate of 7.76 ± 0.73 spikes/sec at the 8–9 s bin, however, indicating that learning caused persistent firing rate to increase faster (Table 9).
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of YC and YP firing rates.

claim: Neurons from AU animals reached a peak firing rate of 7.00 ± 0.52 spikes/sec at the 8–9 s bin.
source: Neurons from AU animals reached a peak firing rate of 7.00 ± 0.52 spikes/sec at the 8–9 s bin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Neurons from AI only reached a peak firing rate of 5.49 ± 0.54 spikes/sec at the 10–11 s bin.
source: Despite this, neurons from AU rats were able to fire more quickly than AI, who only reached a peak firing rate of 5.49 ± 0.54 spikes/sec at the 10–11 s bin.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: A one phase exponential decay function fit to the rising phase revealed a time constant of 1.60 s for YC, being the fastest to rise in firing rate and a time constant of 3.46 s for AI, being the slowest to rise in firing rate.
source: A one phase exponential decay function fit to the rising phase (0–9 s bins) revealed a time constant of 1.60 s for YC, being the fastest to rise in firing rate and a time constant of 3.46 s for AI, being the slowest to rise in firing rate.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and curve fitting shown in Figure 4D.

claim: The time constants of AU and YP were similar, at 2.50 s and 2.24 s respectively.
source: The time constants of AU and YP were similar, at 2.50 s and 2.24 s respectively (Figure 4C,D).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and curve fitting shown in Figure 4D.

claim: In behaviorally naïve animals, neurons from AN have a slower latency than neurons from YN.
source: In behaviorally naïve animals, neurons from AN have a slower latency than neurons from YN (Table 7).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Table 7.

claim: AI animals have the slowest onset latency.
source: We see this reflected also in AI animals, which have the slowest onset latency.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Table 9.

claim: Successful learning decreased latency, resulting in significantly different onset times between YC and AI.
source: Successful learning, however, decreased latency, resulting in significantly different onset times between YC and AI (Figure 4E; Table 9).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4E and Table 9.

claim: In CA1 neurons, aging has been shown to decrease intrinsic excitability, while successful learning has the opposite effect on neurons from young adult and aged animals.
source: In CA1 neurons, aging has been shown to decrease intrinsic excitability, while successful learning has the opposite effect on neurons from young adult and aged animals (Moyer et al., 1996; Moyer et al., 2000; Disterhoft and Oh, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The postburst AHP is a hyperpolarizing current that mediates a refractory period after a burst of action potentials.
source: The postburst AHP is a hyperpolarizing current that mediates a refractory period after a burst of action potentials.
evidence: This is a definition based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: The postburst AHP can be divided into the medium (mAHP) and slow (sAHP) components.
source: It can be divided into the medium (mAHP) and slow (sAHP) components.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: These two components are mediated by separate Ca2+-dependent K+ currents.
source: These two components are mediated by separate Ca2+-dependent K+ currents (Oh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The mAHP lasts for 50–200 ms after the burst of action potentials and is typically measured at the peak of the AHP.
source: The mAHP lasts for 50–200 ms after the burst of action potentials and is typically measured at the peak of the AHP.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge and methodology.

claim: The mAHP is mediated by the apamin-sensitive SK2 channel.
source: The mAHP is mediated by the apamin-sensitive SK2 channel (Bond et al., 2004; Hammond et al., 2006; Disterhoft and Oh, 2006; McKay et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The sAHP lasts for several seconds after the burst of action potentials and is measured 1 s after the burst of action potentials.
source: The sAHP lasts for several seconds after the burst of action potentials and is measured 1 s after the burst of action potentials.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge and methodology.

claim: The channels that mediate the sAHP have yet to be identified.
source: The channels that mediate the sAHP have yet to be identified.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of scientific knowledge.

claim: The sAHP is not mediated by the same apamin-sensitive SK2 channel that mediates the mAHP, as increasing or knocking out SK2 activity has no effect on the sAHP.
source: However, it is known that it is not mediated by the same apamin-sensitive SK2 channel that mediates the mAHP, as increasing or knocking out SK2 activity has no effect on the sAHP (Bond et al., 2004; Hammond et al., 2006; Disterhoft and Oh, 2006; McKay et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the CA1 region of the hippocampus, the mAHP and sAHP are larger in pyramidal neurons from aged animals compared to young adult animals, indicating decreased excitability.
source: In the CA1 region of the hippocampus, the mAHP and sAHP are larger in pyramidal neurons from aged animals compared to young adult animals, indicating decreased excitability (Power et al., 2002; Matthews et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Neurons from AN rats had a larger postburst AHP compared to neurons from YN rats.
source: Neurons from AN rats had a larger postburst AHP compared to neurons from YN rats (Figure 5B; Table 10).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Table 10.

claim: Pyramidal neurons in LEC III undergo an aging-related reduction in intrinsic excitability, similar to what has been observed in CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: Therefore, pyramidal neurons in LEC III undergo an aging-related reduction in intrinsic excitability, similar to what has been observed in CA1 pyramidal neurons (Tombaugh et al., 2005; Disterhoft and Oh, 2006; Power et al., 2002; Matthews et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data and comparison to previous studies.

claim: The intrinsic excitability in LEC III neurons is altered depending on learning condition.
source: The intrinsic excitability in LEC III neurons is also altered depending on learning condition (mAHP, one-way ANOVA, F3, 39 = 18.55, p<0.0001; sAHP, one-way ANOVA, F3, 39 = 8.680, p=0.0002).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: AI had a larger postburst AHP amplitude compared to AU, YC, and YP.
source: AI had a larger postburst AHP amplitude compared to AU, YC, and YP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Table 11.

claim: YC had a smaller postburst AHP compared to YP.
source: YC had a smaller postburst AHP compared to YP (Figure 5C,D; Table 11).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Table 11.

claim: The postburst AHP amplitude of YP animals were similar to that of behaviorally naïve young adult animals.
source: The postburst AHP amplitude of YP animals were similar to that of behaviorally naïve young adult animals (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Table 12).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures and tables.

claim: The postburst AHP from AU animals were comparable to both YC and YP.
source: The postburst AHP from AU animals were comparable to both YC and YP (Figure 5C,D; Table 11).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5D and Table 11.

claim: Neurons from AI animals are significantly less excitable relative to neurons from AU, YC, and even YP animals.
source: These data indicate that neurons from AI animals are significantly less excitable relative to neurons from AU, YC, and even YP animals.
evidence: This is an inference from the postburst AHP data.

claim: There is a positive correlation between learning ability and postburst AHP amplitude amongst the AU and AI group.
source: We have also observed a positive correlation between learning ability and postburst AHP amplitude amongst the AU and AI group, indicating the relationship between learning and intrinsic excitability (Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The correlation between learning ability and postburst AHP amplitude was not present amongst the YC animals.
source: The correlation was not present, however, amongst the YC animals.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Muscarinic activation in LEC III neurons has been demonstrated to eliminate the postburst AHP.
source: Muscarinic activation in LEC III neurons, as is the case in these series of experiments, has been demonstrated to eliminate the postburst AHP.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge from previous studies.

claim: Following a burst of action potentials, instead of an AHP, there is a depolarization of the membrane potential above the baseline, known as the afterdepolarization (ADP).
source: Following a burst of action potentials, then, instead of an AHP, there is a depolarization of the membrane potential above the baseline. This is known as the afterdepolarization (ADP) (Figure 6A,C).
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge and illustrated in the figures.

claim: The ADP allows the neuron to reach spontaneous firing threshold during an up-state and fire action potentials, while the PP allows the firing to persist.
source: The ADP allows the neuron to reach spontaneous firing threshold during an up-state and fire action potentials, while the PP allows the firing to persist.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional properties of ADP and PP.

claim: The ADP amplitude evoked from neurons of AN rats was smaller compared to the peak of the ADP evoked from neurons of YN animals.
source: In behaviorally naive animals, the ADP peak amplitude evoked from neurons of AN rats was smaller compared to the peak of the ADP evoked from neurons of YN animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Table 13.

claim: The area of the ADP and PP was smaller for neurons from aged animals.
source: The area of the ADP and PP was also revealed to be smaller for neurons from aged animals (Figure 6B; Table 13).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6B and Table 13.

claim: When the ADP was evoked from YC neurons, the peak amplitude of the ADP from YC neurons was largest.
source: Therefore, it is not surprising that when the ADP was evoked from YC neurons (250 ms train of 20 Hz, 10 mV more hyperpolarized than spontaneous firing), the peak amplitude of the ADP from YC neurons was largest.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Table 14.

claim: The area of the ADP and PP was largest in YC.
source: The area of the ADP and PP was also largest in YC. (Amplitude: one-way ANOVA, F3,39 = 29.73, p<0.0001) (AUC: one-way ANOVA F3,39 = 15.88, p<0.0001) (Figure 6C,D; Table 14) (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Table 15).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Table 14.

claim: Neurons from AI animals have ADPs that are smallest in terms of amplitude.
source: In contrast, neurons from AI animals, having consistently the lowest probability of persistent firing compared to YC, YP, and AU, have ADPs that are smallest in terms of amplitude.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Table 14.

claim: The area of the ADP and PP from AI animals was smallest.
source: The area of their ADP and PP was also smallest (Figure 6C,D; Table 14).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6D and Table 14.

claim: The ADP size of neurons from AI animals was similar to neurons from AN animals.
source: The ADP size of neurons from AI animals was similar to neurons from AN animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 1; Table 15).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in supplementary figures and tables.

claim: ADP size had an effect on the probability, onset latency, and persistent firing rate.
source: Further analyses revealed that ADP size had an effect on the probability, onset latency, and persistent firing rate.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analyses shown in Figure 6E.

claim: An ADP amplitude of ~4 mV was the boundary which determined successful or unsuccessful firing, with amplitudes at or above 4 mV allowing a neuron to successfully persistently fire.
source: An ADP amplitude of ~4 mV was the boundary which determined successful or unsuccessful firing, with amplitudes at or above 4 mV allowing a neuron to successfully persistently fire (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The ADP amplitude was positively correlated with mean persistent firing rate.
source: The ADP amplitude was also positively correlated with mean persistent firing rate (Pearson, r = 0.6265, p<0.0001), indicating that a larger ADP size allowed for the neuron to fire more quickly.
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A larger ADP size allowed for the neuron to fire more quickly.
source: The ADP amplitude was also positively correlated with mean persistent firing rate (Pearson, r = 0.6265, p<0.0001), indicating that a larger ADP size allowed for the neuron to fire more quickly.
evidence: This is an inference from the positive correlation between ADP amplitude and firing rate.

claim: ADP amplitude was negatively correlated with onset latency.
source: Finally, ADP amplitude was also negatively correlated with onset latency (Pearson, r = −0.4291, p=0.0029), indicating that a larger ADP size allowed the neuron to start firing earlier in the sweep (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6E.

claim: A larger ADP size allowed the neuron to start firing earlier in the sweep.
source: Finally, ADP amplitude was also negatively correlated with onset latency (Pearson, r = −0.4291, p=0.0029), indicating that a larger ADP size allowed the neuron to start firing earlier in the sweep (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is an inference from the negative correlation between ADP amplitude and onset latency.

claim: The ADP size is significantly positively correlated with learning ability amongst AU and AI animals, but not amongst YC animals.
source: Just as we observed with persistent firing rate and postburst AHP amplitude, the ADP size is significantly positively correlated with learning ability amongst AU and AI animals, but not amongst YC animals (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Previous studies have shown that the ADP and PP that generate persistent firing in LEC III and V are mediated by an activity-dependent Ca2+ influx into the neuron.
source: Previous studies have shown that the ADP and PP that generate persistent firing in LEC III and V are mediated by an activity-dependent Ca2+ influx into the neuron (Tahvildari et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The initial current injection to evoke persistent firing generates an influx of Ca2+ into the cell body, which may activate cation currents, including a regenerative current that underlies the PP.
source: The initial current injection to evoke persistent firing generates an influx of Ca2+ into the cell body, which may activate cation currents, including a regenerative current that underlies the PP (Fraser and MacVicar, 1996).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: The ADP and PP were eliminated in neurons from YN animals as well as in YC when CdCl2 was bath applied.
source: We evoked the ADP and PP by holding the membrane potential 10 mV more hyperpolarized than spontaneous firing and found that the ADP and PP were eliminated in neurons from YN animals as well as in YC (ADP: RM ANOVA, pre-post F1,6 = 28.09, p=0.0018; pre-post x group F1,6 = 4.521, p=0.0776) (AUC: pre-post RM ANOVA, F1,6 = 64.31, p=0.0002; pre-post x group F1,6 = 18.64, p=0.0050) (Figure 7; Table 16).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7 and Table 16.

claim: Abolishment of the ADP and PP eliminated persistent firing.
source: Abolishment of the ADP and PP eliminated persistent firing, as evoked by a 250 ms long 20 Hz train of current pulses (Wilcoxon, W = −36.00, p=0.0078).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: The enhanced ADP and PP of LEC III neurons from YC are dependent on Ca2+.
source: These data suggest that, like neurons of YN animals, the enhanced ADP and PP of LEC III neurons from YC are also dependent on Ca2+.
evidence: This is an inference from the CdCl2 experiment results.

claim: A learning-related increase in the size of the ADP in neurons from both aged and young adult animals allowed for the gap between a more hyperpolarized membrane holding potential and spontaneous firing threshold to be more easily overcome than in control animals.
source: Although the persistent firing of neurons from aged animals was less robust, a learning-related increase in the size of the ADP in neurons from both aged and young adult animals allowed for the gap between a more hyperpolarized membrane holding potential and spontaneous firing threshold to be more easily overcome than in control animals.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data on ADP and persistent firing.

claim: A learning-related increase in ADP size may allow for persistent firing to occur more easily following learning, which may be important for the expression and consolidation of the memory.
source: Functionally, this may allow for persistent firing to occur more easily following learning, which may be important for the expression and consolidation of the memory.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: A learning-related increase in ADP size increases the rate of persistent firing within the theta range.
source: The other effect of a learning-related increase in ADP size is to increase the rate of persistent firing within the theta range.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing increased firing rates with learning.

claim: Theta-modulation in the LEC has been shown to be relevant for task-specific actions, such as running.
source: Theta-modulation in the LEC has been shown to be relevant for task-specific actions, such as running (Deshmukh et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: A previous study has shown theta-locking of LEC III neurons when the animal attends to sensory cues during an associative learning task.
source: A previous study has also shown theta-locking of LEC III neurons when the animal attends to sensory cues during an associative learning task (Igarashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: It has been hypothesized that persistent firing rate could provide a phase code for changes to object features in the continuous dimension, such that an increase in persistent firing rate could allow for a phase shift in firing to encode continuous dimensions.
source: It has been hypothesized that persistent firing rate could provide a phase code for changes to object features in the continuous dimension, such that an increase in persistent firing rate could allow for a phase shift in firing to encode continuous dimensions (Hasselmo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous work supported by citation.

claim: An increase in persistent firing rate during trace eyeblink conditioning could allow for the properties of the stimuli (e.g. tone, timing) to be properly encoded so that a more precise behavioral response can be elicited.
source: In this manner, an increase in persistent firing rate during trace eyeblink conditioning could allow for the properties of the stimuli (e.g. tone, timing) to be properly encoded so that a more precise behavioral response can be elicited.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of increased firing rate.

claim: The LEC has been shown to increase theta synchronization with both the hippocampus and the prefrontal cortex following CS onset during the acquisition phase of trace eyeblink conditioning.
source: The LEC has been shown to increase theta synchronization with both the hippocampus and the prefrontal cortex following CS onset during the acquisition phase of trace eyeblink conditioning.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citation to Takehara-Nishiuchi et al., 2011.

claim: Theta oscillations between the LEC and the prefrontal cortex become strongly synchronized as the animal acquires trace eyeblink conditioning, and continue this synchronized activity through encoding and consolidation.
source: Theta oscillations between the LEC and the prefrontal cortex, in particular, become strongly synchronized as the animal acquires trace eyeblink conditioning, and continue this synchronized activity through encoding and consolidation (Takehara-Nishiuchi et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Lesions to the temporoammonic pathway have been shown to eliminate consolidation of a hippocampus-dependent memory.
source: In fact, lesions to the temporoammonic pathway have been shown to eliminate consolidation of a hippocampus-dependent memory (Remondes and Schuman, 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: An increase in persistent firing rate may be the result of successful acquisition of trace eyeblink conditioning and may support consolidation of the newly acquired association into long-term memory.
source: An increase in persistent firing rate, therefore, may also be the result of successful acquisition of trace eyeblink conditioning and may support consolidation of the newly acquired association into long-term memory.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of increased firing rate.

claim: Neurons from aged animals that were trained on trace eyeblink conditioning but failed to learn the paradigm had a reduced capacity for persistent firing even compared to neurons from young adult control animals.
source: We observed that neurons from aged animals that were trained on trace eyeblink conditioning but failed to learn the paradigm had a reduced capacity for persistent firing even compared to neurons from young adult control animals (i.e. YP).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing AI to YP groups.

claim: An aging-related decrease in persistent firing ability may contribute to the learning impairments observed in the aging population.
source: An aging-related decrease in persistent firing ability may, therefore, contribute to the learning impairments that we and others have observed in the aging population (Knuttinen et al., 2001).
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between persistent firing deficits and learning impairments.

claim: Although neurons from AU animals were able to persistently fire, they were not able to fire as robustly as neurons from YC animals.
source: At the same time, although neurons from AU animals were able to persistently fire, they were not able to fire as robustly as neurons from YC animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing AU and YC groups.

claim: When the gap between the neuronal membrane holding potential and spontaneous firing threshold was increased, neurons from aged animals that successfully learned were unable to reach the ceiling effect that neurons from young animals that successfully learned were able to reach.
source: When the gap between the neuronal membrane holding potential and spontaneous firing threshold was increased, neurons from aged animals that successfully learned were unable to reach the ceiling effect that neurons from young animals that successfully learned were able to reach.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing AU and YC at different membrane potentials.

claim: The firing rate of neurons from AU animals was slower than those from young animals that learned.
source: Their firing rate was also slower than those from young animals that learned.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data comparing firing rates of AU and YC.

claim: Neurons from AU animals had a slower time to reach peak firing rate compared to neurons from YC animals.
source: They also had a slower time to reach peak firing rate compared to neurons from YC animals.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on time constants and peak firing times.

claim: A slower time to reach peak firing may make it more difficult for neurons to be included in an ensemble to help bridge the trace interval.
source: A slower time to reach peak firing may make it more difficult for neurons to be included in an ensemble to help bridge the trace interval.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional consequences of slower firing dynamics.

claim: A slower time to reach peak firing may result in desynchronization within the LEC network of theta and other rhythms that are necessary for hippocampus-dependent learning, such as gamma.
source: Alternatively, it may also result in desynchronization within the LEC network of theta and other rhythms that are necessary for hippocampus-dependent learning, such as gamma (Igarashi et al., 2014).
evidence: This is speculation about the functional consequences supported by citation.

claim: Although neurons from unimpaired aged animals were still able to persistently fire, they were also affected by the changes in neuronal properties that are associated with aging.
source: As a result, although neurons from unimpaired aged animals were still able to persistently fire, they were also affected by the changes in neuronal properties that are associated with aging.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental data showing reduced firing capacity in AU compared to YC.

claim: The ability of AU animals to achieve the same level of learning behaviorally may be the result of compensatory mechanisms in other regions.
source: The ability of AU animals to achieve the same level of learning behaviorally may be the result of compensatory mechanisms in other regions.
evidence: This is speculation about compensatory mechanisms.

claim: These regions may include those that are functionally connected to the LEC, such as the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus.
source: These regions may include those that are functionally connected to the LEC, such as the prefrontal cortex and the hippocampus.
evidence: This is speculation about which regions might provide compensation.

claim: In the CA1 region of the hippocampus, if an aged animal is able to acquire a hippocampus-dependent task such as trace eyeblink conditioning, the excitability of the neurons increases.
source: In the CA1 region of the hippocampus, for example, if an aged animal is able to acquire a hippocampus-dependent task such as trace eyeblink conditioning, the excitability of the neurons increases (Moyer et al., 2000; Matthews et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: The excitability of CA1 neurons from aged animals that successfully learned is comparable to those of a young animal who successfully acquired trace eyeblink conditioning.
source: Moreover, the excitability of these neurons is comparable to those of a young animal who successfully acquired trace eyeblink conditioning, unlike in neurons of LEC III.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies and contrasted with current findings.

claim: The firing ability of CA1 neurons may serve to help compensate for the less robust persistent firing in LEC III neurons of AU animals.
source: The firing ability of CA1 neurons, therefore, may serve to help compensate for the less robust persistent firing in LEC III neurons of AU animals.
evidence: This is speculation about compensatory mechanisms.

claim: The excitability of CA1 neurons may be a better determinant of successful learning in aging than that of LEC III neurons.
source: It also seems that the excitability of CA1 neurons may be a better determinant of successful learning in aging than that of LEC III neurons.
evidence: This is an inference from the comparison of CA1 and LEC III excitability changes.

claim: The differences in excitability changes across separate regions of an interconnected memory network point to individually weighted contributions to the development of hippocampus-dependent memory.
source: The differences in excitability changes across separate regions of an interconnected memory network point to individually weighted contributions to the development of hippocampus-dependent memory.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed regional differences.

claim: Although there may be excitability differences in each region as a result of aging, they may not be equal contributors to memory acquisition.
source: Although there may be excitability differences in each region as a result of aging, they may not be equal contributors to memory acquisition.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed regional differences.

claim: While learning increased the ADP, it decreased the AHP.
source: The changes we have observed in excitability in LEC III are also reflected in the AHP. While learning increased the ADP, it decreased the AHP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on ADP and AHP measurements.

claim: Aging had the effect of decreasing the ADP and increasing the AHP.
source: Aging, on the other hand, had the effect of decreasing the ADP and increasing the AHP.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data on ADP and AHP measurements.

claim: An inverse relationship between the AHP and the ADP may exist in LEC III pyramidal neurons.
source: As a result, an inverse relationship between the AHP and the ADP may exist in LEC III pyramidal neurons, with a smaller AHP (i.e. following learning) allowing for the development of a larger ADP, and a larger AHP (i.e. as a result of aging) impeding the development of a larger ADP.
evidence: This is an inference from the observed opposing changes in AHP and ADP.

claim: A previous study performed in CA1 neurons has shown that elimination of the postburst AHP allows for the development of an ADP.
source: A previous study performed in CA1 neurons has in fact shown that elimination of the postburst AHP allows for the development of an ADP.
evidence: This is supported by the subsequent citation to Wu et al., 2004.

claim: The presence of the AHP inhibited the temporal summation of the mechanism supporting the ADP.
source: The presence of the AHP inhibited the temporal summation of the mechanism supporting the ADP (Wu et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Both the AHP and ADP are mediated by Ca2+ influx following a burst of action potentials.
source: Although the exact channels and mechanisms that underlie the ADP are still unknown, what is known is that both the AHP and ADP are mediated by Ca2+ influx following a burst of action potentials.
evidence: This is based on established scientific knowledge.

claim: Postburst Ca2+ influx, via voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, activates Ca2+ activated K+ channels, which generate the AHP.
source: Postburst Ca2+ influx, via voltage-gated Ca2+ channels, activates Ca2+ activated K+ channels, which generate the AHP (Bond et al., 2004; Disterhoft and Oh, 2006; McKay et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: If the AHP is suppressed, as with neuromodulators such as acetylcholine, Ca2+-activated cationic conductances (e.g. CAN channels), also activated by postburst Ca2+ influx, may present themselves, resulting in the development of an ADP.
source: However, if the AHP is suppressed, as with neuromodulators such as acetylcholine, Ca2+-activated cationic conductances (e.g. CAN channels), also activated by postburst Ca2+ influx, may present themselves, resulting in the development of an ADP (Tahvildari et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Further experiments are needed to elucidate the interaction between the AHP and the ADP in LEC III pyramidal neurons, and how learning and aging affect both mechanisms.
source: Further experiments are needed to elucidate the interaction between the AHP and the ADP in LEC III pyramidal neurons, however, and how learning and aging affect both mechanisms in order to support and inhibit persistent firing, respectively.
evidence: This is a statement about future research needs.

claim: The functional role that persistent firing plays during trace eyeblink conditioning and other temporal associative tasks is yet to be determined in vivo.
source: Finally, although we have established that learning and aging differentially affect persistent firing, the functional role that persistent firing plays during trace eyeblink conditioning and other temporal associative tasks is yet to be determined in vivo.
evidence: This is a statement about the limitations of the current study.

claim: One possible role of persistent firing is to enhance the activity of their direct downstream target, CA1 pyramidal neurons.
source: One possible role is to enhance the activity of their direct downstream target, CA1 pyramidal neurons.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of persistent firing.

claim: Temporoammonic activity from LEC III to CA1 has the ability to modulate Schaffer-Collateral (SC) evoked CA1 spiking activity.
source: Temporoammonic activity from LEC III to CA1 has the ability to modulate Schaffer-Collateral (SC) evoked CA1 spiking activity (Remondes and Schuman, 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: Persistent firing in LEC III neurons may enhance SC input to CA1 neurons, allowing for CA1 neurons to be more responsive to convergent CS and US information that is provided via the tri-synaptic pathway.
source: As such, persistent firing in LEC III neurons may enhance SC input to CA1 neurons, allowing for CA1 neurons to be more responsive to convergent CS and US information that is provided via the tri-synaptic pathway.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of persistent firing.

claim: Previous studies from our laboratory have shown an increase in CA1 activity in response to both the CS and the US in vivo.
source: Evidence for this comes from previous studies from our laboratory, which have shown an increase in CA1 activity in response to both the CS and the US in vivo (McEchron and Disterhoft, 1997; McEchron and Disterhoft, 1999).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Persistent firing in LEC III may serve to enhance the processing of salient stimuli within CA1 neurons, allowing for the successful acquisition of trace eyeblink conditioning.
source: Therefore, persistent firing in LEC III may serve to enhance the processing of salient stimuli within CA1 neurons, allowing for the successful acquisition of trace eyeblink conditioning.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional role of persistent firing.

claim: The prevailing hypothesis in the literature is that persistent firing supports a 'memory' of the CS during the trace interval, so that the association between the CS and the US can be made.
source: The prevailing hypothesis in the literature, however, is that persistent firing supports a 'memory' of the CS during the trace interval, so that the association between the CS and the US can be made (Kitamura et al., 2015; Zylberberg and Strowbridge, 2017).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from the literature supported by citations.

claim: Previous in vivo work has shown that persistent activity in the prefrontal cortex bridges the delay period during a working memory task, and inhibition of persistent activity impairs acquisition.
source: Previous in vivo work has shown that persistent activity in the prefrontal cortex bridges the delay period during a working memory task, and inhibition of persistent activity impairs acquisition (Fuster, 1972; Liu et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: On the level of individual neurons, persistent firing ability may support the trace by spanning the entire trace interval.
source: On the level of individual neurons, persistent firing ability as we have described here may support the trace by spanning the entire trace interval (Constantinidis et al., 2018)
evidence: This is speculation supported by citation.

claim: Persistent firing may allow the neuron to participate in an ensemble pattern of activity that allows the trace to be bridged.
source: or allow the neuron to participate in an ensemble pattern of activity that allows the trace to be bridged (Miller et al., 2018; Lundqvist et al., 2018).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations.

claim: Persistent firing in LEC III is strongly suggested to support the acquisition of trace eyeblink conditioning.
source: Either way, persistent firing in LEC III is strongly suggested to support the acquisition of trace eyeblink conditioning.
evidence: This is an inference from the experimental findings and literature.

claim: Blocking activity of the LEC has been shown to inhibit temporal associative learning.
source: Blocking activity of the LEC has been shown to inhibit temporal associative learning (Morrissey et al., 2012; Wilson et al., 2013)
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: In the medial entorhinal cortex, inhibition of layer III activity to the CA1 region has been shown to impair trace fear conditioning.
source: and in the medial entorhinal cortex, inhibition of layer III activity to the CA1 region has been shown to impair trace fear conditioning (Suh et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous work.

claim: These data suggest that persistent firing in LEC III is a crucial mechanism in supporting the formation of the temporal association during trace eyeblink conditioning.
source: Together, these data suggest that persistent firing in LEC III is a crucial mechanism in supporting the formation of the temporal association during trace eyeblink conditioning.
evidence: This is an inference from the current findings and cited literature.

claim: What we have established is that persistent firing is a mechanism that is, at the very least, important for acquiring trace eyeblink conditioning.
source: Whatever the functional role of persistent firing may be in supporting trace eyeblink conditioning, what we have established is that it is a mechanism that is, at the very least, important for acquiring this temporal associative paradigm.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: Successful acquisition of trace eyeblink conditioning enhances persistent firing ability in both young adult and aged animals.
source: Successful acquisition of trace eyeblink conditioning enhances persistent firing ability in both young adult and aged animals
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the experimental findings.

claim: An aged-related decrease in persistent firing ability may lead to learning impairments in acquiring the paradigm.
source: while an aged-related decrease in persistent firing ability may lead to learning impairments in acquiring the paradigm.
evidence: This is an inference from the correlation between persistent firing deficits and learning impairments.

claim: Future studies should examine the extent to which persistent firing is necessary for temporal associative learning.
source: Along with examining the functional role of persistent firing in acquiring temporal associative learning in vivo, future studies should also examine the extent to which persistent firing is necessary.
evidence: This is a statement about future research directions.

claim: Such studies would pave the way to better understanding the neural network that underlies the acquisition of this type of complex task.
source: Such studies would pave the way to better understanding the neural network that underlies the acquisition of this type of complex task.
evidence: This is speculation about the value of future research.
